title: The Science of Reading Has Won the Argument. Has It Won the Classroom?
author: Unknown Author
summary: This Fordham Institute analysis examines the persistent implementation gap between policy adoption of reading science and actual classroom practice. While nearly every state has passed science-of-reading-aligned legislation and most teachers favor phonics, only half of K–3 teachers implement fully structured instruction. Most troubling is the high-poverty paradox: disadvantaged schools report greater training yet demonstrate weaker teacher knowledge. The study indicts teacher preparation programs, finding preservice education correlates with lower knowledge than on-the-job learning. Mississippi's two-decade marathon of systematic teacher development provides a contrasting model of sustained institutional change.
points: Policy victories do not automatically translate to instructional change; despite nearly universal state adoption, only half of K–3 teachers use fully structured approaches, with one-third still using discredited methods.

Teachers relying solely on preservice training demonstrate significantly weaker reading science knowledge than those acquiring it on the job; teacher preparation programs miseducate about foundational literacy instruction.

High-poverty schools report more training yet demonstrate weaker teacher knowledge, suggesting inadequate training quality or insufficient baseline preparation, with dire consequences for disadvantaged students.
Curriculum choice shapes teacher knowledge; those using science-aligned programs demonstrate stronger understanding, indicating curriculum functions as a knowledge-building tool.
Mississippi's 20-year success relied on policy coherence, monthly district monitoring, direct superintendent accountability, and persistent follow-up—not merely legislation.
quotes: Teachers who rely on their preservice training know less about the science of reading than those who learn it on the job.
